title: Points of convergence - music meets mathematics
venue: More UK Success Stories in Industrial Mathematics
extended_summary:
This chapter discusses a piece of pure mathematics on phase-locking in the Arnold family of circle maps and uses it as a case study for how frontier research can influence creative collaboration. The central mathematical question is whether hyperbolic parameters are dense in the Arnold family, meaning that stable behavior can be found arbitrarily close to chaotic behavior. The paper explains the result that hyperbolic maps are dense and outlines the key ideas behind the proof, including complex extension, rigidity, and perturbation arguments.

The second half describes a collaboration between the author and composer Emily Howard during her 2015 artist-in-residence appointment in Liverpool’s mathematics department. The collaboration turned research ideas into numerical datasets that inspired musical works such as Orbits, Torus, sphere, and Antisphere. The paper presents this as an example of research-led creative exchange rather than an educational intervention.

The paper’s main conclusion is that mathematically rich, conceptually accessible research can support productive interdisciplinary collaboration when there is a shared language and a carefully chosen topic. It argues that the success of the collaboration came from Howard’s mathematical background and the suitability of the hyperbolicity result for creative interpretation, including its themes of stability near chaos and the role of hidden structure in the proof.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/mathematical research chapter describing dynamical systems results and a music collaboration, not an empirical study of an educational or AI intervention. There is no student sample, no comparison condition, and no outcome measurement relevant to K-12 learning.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no direct educational or AI intervention effects and provides no evidence of impact on learners or schools. Its relevance to the retrieval topic is only indirect through a non-educational collaboration narrative.
